# Trade unions and collective bargaining (`trade_unions_collective_bargaining`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by free_press, representative_government, social_insurance
- Core idea: Workers in one trade or workplace combine, pay dues into a common fund, and bargain as a body over wages, hours and safety, with the strike as their last resort. One worker who refuses bad terms is replaced; all of them together cannot be, so bargaining power becomes roughly equal. The fund that pays members during a strike, sickness or unemployment is what holds a union together. For lasting results the right to combine must be lawful, agreements written and binding, and disputes brought to arbitration before a stoppage.
- Pitfalls:
  - Calling a strike with no fund and no law behind it: for most of history combination was conspiracy, punished by prison, transportation or death
  - Breaking machines instead of bargaining over them invites the army (Luddites, 1811–1816)
  - Assuming strikes are modern: Egyptian tomb builders stopped work over unpaid rations around 1157 BC
  - A union that controls entry to a trade behaves like a guild and shuts out the unskilled, women and newcomers
- History: egypt: c. 1157 BC – workmen of Deir el-Medina lay down tools over late rations under Ramesses III (Turin Strike Papyrus), the first recorded strike; rome: occasional recorded work stoppages by bakers, builders and mint workers under the Empire; china: Qing (18th c.) – strikes of Suzhou textile workers and stone inscriptions banning them; europe: 1378 – revolt of the Ciompi, Florence's unorganised wool workers; 14th–18th c. journeymen's associations; 1799–1800 British Combination Acts ban unions, repealed 1824; 1871 Trade Union Act legalises them; americas: 1842 – Commonwealth v. Hunt (Massachusetts) holds unions lawful; 1935 Wagner Act
- Read:
  - Sidney Webb & Beatrice Webb, The History of Trade Unionism (1894)
  - E. P. Thompson, The Making of the English Working Class (1963)
